utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning everyone. Good morning, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. May I introduce to you Jade Werkmeister, who is from the University of Melbourne in Australia, who is joining us this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Helgers. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: My full name is Marcus Martinus Emanuel Helgers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in 1995 you held the rank of captain in the Dutch air force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, and we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You provided a signed statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor in August 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 22677 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, is that your statement at the bottom of the page 1?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. Sorry. Is it right that you've had an opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there's one correction and a couple of clarifications that you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, as I've made them in your presence last Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The reference to the 16th of June, 1995, should read 18 June 1995 as is stated in the paragraph above?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With respect to the clarifications in the first paragraph on page 3, there's a reference to Major Westlund being forced to contact UN headquarters Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you wish to state that you no longer remember and therefore cannot be sure whether he did that contact from Jahorina or from Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph on page 3, there's a reference to being taken from a point at Jahorina a distance of 5, 6, or 700 metres to the radar station. You wish to clarify that you cannot be sure of the distance in metres but that it took you approximately 15 minutes walking in the snow?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that Ms. Sutherland slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With that correction and the clarifications, do you confirm that the statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The statement is accurate with the clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today about the same series of events, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, with one remark: That it has been 16 years ago, so it might be that some small details I do not recall as clearly as I did 16 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender 65 ter 22677 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I will now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. In 1995, in April, Marcus Helgers was a captain in the Dutch air force stationed near Kasindo, south of Sarajevo, as a United Nations Military Observer, that is, an UNMO. On the 26th of May, 1995, the witness together with five other UNMOs deployed to the same observation post, were ceased by armed soldiers and driven to a guard post in Grbavica. There they were forced to change into civilian clothes. The six UNMOs were then driven to the police station in Pale, then to a cafe bar in Pale, and subsequently taken to the Jahorina radar station where he was held by the Bosnian Serb forces for 20 days. While being held, the witness received threats on his life. At one point, the deputy team leader of the six UNMOs was forced to contact UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo and tell them that the VRS would kill some of them if NATO continued with air-strikes. Early the following morning, 27 May 1995, the witness was taken with another UNMO to the roof of the tower near the main radar dome where he was held for approximately two hours. UNMOs were taken to the tower in shifts of two men for approximately two hours each. After being held at Jahorina radar station for 20 days, he was then taken with two UNMOs to a military police station in Pale and then to the military barracks at Koran-Pale where they were detained for a further four days. Their release from Pale on 18 June 1995 was overseen by Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. Mr. Koljevic spoke to the military observers on that day and also Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic spoke. Indjic then signed a document handing them over to the security forces. The UNMOs were then driven by bus to Pale where they met with the "security chief of Milosevic." They were taken to Zvornik and then on to Novi Sad. The following day, 19 June 1995, the witness was taken from Novi Sad to Belgrade airport where he flew to Zagreb. That concludes the summary, Your Honour. I would now like to clarify a few details and ask some specific questions about the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, what date were you first deployed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I -- I entered the mission in Zagreb on the 26th of April. I was flown to Sarajevo around or on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I was to be stationed at the enclave of Zepa, but due to the fact that at that moment it was not possible to -- to deploy me in that area, I was temporarily assigned to the UNMO station in Kasindo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many were in your team and if you recall what nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The team leader was Spanish, the deputy team leader was Swedish and the total amount of people they changed. At the moment, on 26th, when I was taken hostage, we were six.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Our duties was to -- to monitor the cease-fire, monitor the weapon collection points, to report on any shelling coming in or going out and generally investigate any reports about shooting incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: We were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point was your freedom of movement restricted?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Almost constantly during the period, so the fact is we did very little patrolling because, virtually from day one, there were very severe movement restrictions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, you state that on the 26th of May, the deputy to the local battalion commander --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- came to the observation post at around 1330 hours?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what he said?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: He said that there had been some air-strikes and that we were given house arrests and that we were to stay in the -- in the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said on that page that he came back at around 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you recall him saying when he came back the second time?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I have to make one clarification. I'm not completely sure if it was a deputy commander or a security officer. I do know what he said quite clearly because that's engraved in my memory. He said there had been more -- more strikes, and that we were having house arrests and that we should not go outside, and that if we were to go outside, we would be shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From there you were taken by two armed soldiers to a guard post at Grbavica. That's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That was later. It was at around 4.00 or something later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did these soldiers identify themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: No. However, they were dressed in partial uniforms and -- well, sufficiently to identify them as Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Chamber what occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: At the moment that I was taken hostage or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you were at the guard post at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, we were put in a, well, in a basement at the -- the command post was a basement of an apartment block. We were put there under guard and then -- it was command post. People started making phone calls. I don't know any Serbian-Croatian. However, I could hear that it was about us and about uniforms. Then we were forced to take off all of our uniforms and we were forced to take on civilian clothes. In my case a training suit that I bought in Zagreb, and the other colleagues, whatever private clothes they had, except Major Bello Abdul Razak from Nigeria. He did not have any civilian clothes. He was forced to put on a former Yugoslav Army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you think was going to happen to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Because I was quite afraid, worried to be sure, we were very close to the confrontation line and the thought had occurred to me was that since it was very irregular being taken off -- that we had to take off our uniform, that we were going to be sent over the confrontation line, presumably to be shot by the opposing party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to a time after you arrived in Pale from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated on page 2 of your statement that when you were taken to Pale, that you met some UNMOs from the 7 Lima team who had been captured earlier.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said there was a young Bosnian Serb soldier who spoke good English.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall what that Bosnian Serb soldier said?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Very clearly. He said that we were hostages for the Bosnian Serbs, that we were going to be station -- brought to Jahorina radar station where we were going to be used as human shields. He further told us that if there was any air-strike by NATO, one of us would be shot, and that if there was an air-strike at the radar station and any of us were to survive, we would all be shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said that you were going to be taken to Jahorina and used as human shields, what did you understand this to be mean?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: For me it was quite clear that we were going to be placed at the station so that if a NATO air attack were to take place, we would be hit, too, and furthermore, as he stated, that if there was an air-strike at another location in Bosnia on Bosnia Serb troops, or forces, or units, that one of us would be shot. And anyway, if there was an attack on radio station and we were to be survive, we would all be executed afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel make a pause after the witness has answered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that you were then taken in a vehicle and up to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You have mentioned in your statement that a number of you were mistreated in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then you had to walk a certain distance. Were any of you mistreated along the way?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: In the -- when -- at the foot of the radio station was a sort of hotel where I was told it had been used for -- for Olympic Games earlier. We were handed over from the regular car. We were into a military bus, small bus, by -- and we were guarded by -- transferred to the guard of three Bosnian Serb guards. One of them was quite drunk. The other one was not sober. You could see it in their behaviour. You could smell it on them. And the driver was at least more or less sober, I think. In the car they started asking questions, and when Major Bello Abdul Razak from Nigeria, when he didn't answer quickly enough, they hit him with the butt of a Kalashnikov rifle in his head from behind. And later on, Major Westlund, from Sweden, he -- because he didn't answer correctly or quickly enough he was also butted, but in the shoulder. Later on when we left the car and had to walk to the radar station, we were kicked a few times, but not very extremely hard, just to force us along.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that when you got there you were taken to the barracks and taken to a room.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the next morning, this is on page 3, that is the 27th of May, 1995, the two of you were taken to a tower 15 metres from the main radar dome. Can you just describe the -- the area?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Okay. It was -- it was a mountain top, quite high. I do remember very clearly that when we came -- as I told you, we had to walk the last part. The area was largely covered with snow, not completely. In fact, when we left 20 days later, it was still some patches of snow left. The radar station at the bottom, about 200 metres below the domes themselves, there was sort of barracks which was used as sleeping area, command post, I don't know exactly. Then there was a winding road up -- upwards towards the radar itself. There were two domes, big, white, multi-facetted domes, a big one and a small one. There was an entrance to the area just below the main -- the main radar dome in which we were forced to enter, and we were taken to the first room on the right side. What I do remember quite clearly is that there was also sort of guard tower about 15 metres' distance from the main dome, and when we were taken to -- to the radar and put in -- sort of in -- under the main radar dome, afterwards at -- two of us at a turn were taken outside and put on -- in my case on the top of the radar -- of the guard tower, which is very close to the main radar dome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On page 3 you said that Pale Television arrived with some UNMOs for filming.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see these UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I did not see these UNMOs because at that time I was underground, under the radar dome, and two other colleagues at that time at the watch tower, they were taken in and they told me they had seen Pale TV arrive with some -- some uniformed UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want you to view a brief video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The first part of the clip is 65 ter number 40202D.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise anything in that shot? We've paused at 40:57. We started the clip at 40:43 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, it was this radar dome or one -- well, the almost identical twin of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play it again -- continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, can I intervene. Is it your plan to do without transcript, without those being read out?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the visual that I want the witness to look at. If we could continue, and if we could pause it at 41:40, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise who is in that shot?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a Brazilian UNMO named Harley or Harvey. I recall him very clearly because I met him later on in Pale when the UNMOs were collected for later release.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is Harley his first or last name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: As far as I know it's his last name but I'm not sure. I knew him as Harley or Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can pause at 42:49, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise the gentleman in that shot?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, he's Polish, but I don't, I don't recall him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can continue and then pause at 43:06.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you recognise in that shot?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, that's the radar dome. It's the one I was held at or, well, its twin. What you can also see, I think, in the background are the snow patches that I was mentioning earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play again and pause at 43:14, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- that's the smaller dome I was telling you about. There was a bigger dome and there was a smaller dome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. The next clip I wish to show you is 65 ter 40202F, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could pause it there, please. That's paused at 44:01.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise who is in that shot?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my colleague, Dutch UNMO. Captain Wilko Ramarkus [phoen] from the Dutch air force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was Ramarkus chained to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: He told me he had been chained to a Bosnian Serb aircraft shelter in or near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender both of those clips. The first clip will be shown with another witness on Friday, and at that point we will be using the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering the entire video-clip or the D part refers to the part you've shown -- you have shown today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I want to tender both clips, the clip of -- at the dome and the clip of the Dutch UNMO that we can see on the screen now. That's 40202D and 40202F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we don't need the time clip because only that part will be tendered. That's my understanding. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2143 and P2144, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, in your statement at page 3, you said that you were held at Jahorina for 20 days, and the room where you were held in, how far was this from the radar tower? You may have mentioned it earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That depends on how you -- if you had to walk it, it goes maybe 40, 50 metres, but it was -- the radar dome, as you could see, was on the top and below it there was an entrance into -- to the area. I didn't see the complete area, of course, because we were taken on the inside in the first door on the right. Walking distance would have been less than 50 metres. I mean, horizontal or vertical distance would have been 20 metres, 25, 30 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who appeared to you to be in charge at the radar station?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: There was a sublieutenant who was in charge. His name was Trafkovic. We met him on the 26th, in the evening, when we arrived at the barracks at the foot of the -- of the radar domes, and he warned us at that time, please, that he was very sorry about the situation, that he warned us not to try to escape especially since the area around the radar station was mined. And later on, I don't recall which day, we were taken downstairs to the barracks at the foot of the radar station, radar dome, where we met with him. He asked us how we were doing and I remember playing two games of chess with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did -- what, if anything, did he say to you about your detention?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: He stated that, as I told you, he was sorry about the situation and he hoped the situation would be resolved and that we would be released quickly. Also, what I remember from the first day, that we had been taken as an order from -- from the Bosnian Serb president.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was something that he told you on the first day?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening. I want to rephrase that. I don't recall exactly he said Bosnian Serb president or Bosnian Serb command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated on page 3 that on the 14th of June, three of you were taken from the Jahorina radar station. Who took you, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The 13th you mean? The 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Okay. The three of us which were left at that time, we were taken to a -- well, it looks to be a sort of hotel complex where we met Captain Manzoor, who was one of the members our team which together -- he, together with Major Westlund, had been separated from us quite quickly after the event, and I was given to understand that he had been -- been used as a human shield at the control centre for the radar station. And after we collected Captain Manzoor we were driven to Pale, where we met the other UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on page 3 of your statement you say on Tuesday, the 13th of June, 1995, Major --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Wojtasiak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Wojtasiak was released.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the following day --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, so it must have been the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- the 14th, the remaining three of you were taken to the hotel complex?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, so it must have been 14th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said Captain Vojvodic was in charge at the barracks. How did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, he gave his name, and some of the other UNMOs who had been longer in -- in -- in the barracks, they had given his name too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, on page 4 of your statement you describe the events on Sunday, the 18th of June, 1995, as to how you came to be released --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- from Bosnia when you met Koljevic and Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I won't go into that now. I'd like you to look at a map, 65 ter 23076. This is a map which -- the map that will appear on the screen has been prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor using 65 ter 19082 as the base map. Overlaid on this map are the different locations in Bosnia where you were held during the period 26 May 1995 to 19 June.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to review this map --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does this map accurately reflect your movements during the period you were held by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this map for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see the -- Kasindo marked with a -- with a black dot and then to Grbavica, over to Pale, down to Jahorina radar station, back to Pale, and then you were taken over to -- in the direction of --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Novi Sad. Thank you. I've finished with that map. There are a number of documents I wish to show and I want to ask you whether certain aspects of these documents are consistent with your experiences.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 09404 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a Main Staff document from the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 26th of May, 1995. There are a number of targets listed there, alleged NATO targets. Are these targets consistent with where you and other UNMOs were subsequently held as hostages?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Just for myself, I was held at the radar station, and I know about my -- my colleague Rabakus [phoen] because he was held at an air base. Two of my colleagues from the same team, Major Westlund and Captain Manzoor, were taken to a command post or radar control post, as I told you before, so that it is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the next document could be brought up, 65 ter 09172.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, this is a Main Staff Army of Republika Srpska document, dated the 27th of May, 1995, which discusses the VRS assessment of where NATO will concentrate their operations, ammunition dumps, fire positions of anti-aircraft defence equipment, artillery, armoured mechanism units and command posts. Again, are these areas consistent with where you and other UNMOs were placed at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: As I told you, I don't know the exact locations of where all the UNMOs were placed, but as far as my recollection is and my personal experience, we were placed at military strategic or vital locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think at the time this -- this document was received you were, in fact, at the radar station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: On the 27th, I was already on the radar station. As I told you, I was taken very early on 27th in the morning from the barracks at the foot of the radio station towards the radio station itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Let the record reflect we're being very generous at this point but we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit P00893 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We see this is dated the 17th of June, 1995. It's an order from the president of the republic, Dr. Karadzic, regarding the release of the remaining UNPROFOR and military observers.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First, you can confirm that you were released on the 18th of June, at least from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, it -- or order number -- point number 2, it refers to the return of personal weapons to UNPROFOR and military observers.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified earlier that UNMOs were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I did not have any weapon bigger than probably a pocket knife, which was taken from me, and as to the return of personal effects, my personal effects were, well, confiscated when I was taken hostage and I never got them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Helgers, what impact, if any, has the period that you were held by the Bosnian Serb forces had upon you?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: At the moment of the -- of the -- of the -- the events, that was quite stressful, and my reaction was that -- was that I put off my emotion, more or less, till arriving on the -- I think it was the 19th in Zagreb, when I entered the mess I had the shakes for about two minutes. After which I had -- well, all my muscles hurt for about a week. Afterwards I had some sleepless nights about two months later. Then I did not have any problems until about 2000 -- 2000, 2001 -- 2001, in fact, when I became quite stressed, recurrences of the events, sleeplessness, irritation, lessened performance, and I was later diagnosed by Dutch military that I had post-traumatic stress disorder. I've been treated for that quite successfully, I think. I had some small recurrences later but they are minor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour. The 65 ter number listed as the first additional exhibit in the 92 ter notification is technically an associated exhibit because it was referred to in the statement. However, I don't seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Helgers. First of all, I would like to thank you for having met with the Defence. I hope this will help us in our effort to be very precise and very expeditious. I would like to thank you for your kindness in that respect. You are a captain in the Dutch air force. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: At the moment of my -- my taking hostage, I was a captain in the air force. At the moment I'm a major in the Dutch Marechaussee, which is a gendarmerie force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your task? What was your mission at your observation post in Kasindo?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: As I stated earlier towards the Prosecution, my task were -- our task, our tasks were to observe the cease-fire, monitor the weapon collection points, and report on any incoming or outgoing shelling, and investigate shooting reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were there for a month prior to the event in question, did you have good relations with the Serbian officers and the local population? What was your relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The -- I did not meet any special hostility. Having said that, I must note that my contacts with Serbian military and Serbian civilians were very limited due to restriction of movement. Furthermore, I was not team leader or deputy team leader in charge of negotiations or dealing with Serbian authorities, police, anyway, or military, sorry. And furthermore, I was placed at the Kasindo station temporarily because I was -- they planned for me to go to Zepa at a later state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there was a major Muslim offensive ongoing, an offensive which was launched on the 1st of May and intensified after the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I do remember that there have been some very -- very -- well, quite intense shelling during a few days during my stay in Kasindo. When I came in Sarajevo it was quite quiet, and afterwards it heated up quite quickly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, on page 2 you say that on that day, around 1330 hours, Serbian soldiers came, and the local commander told you about NATO air-strikes, and that for your own safety you were supposed to stay in house arrest where you would be guarded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The deputy commander, as I recall, to be quite clear, I had not met him before he was pointed out to me by colleagues as being the deputy commander. He stated that there had been some air-strikes and that indeed we were to stay at the -- at our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. An hour and a half later he arrived, and his attitude towards you was somewhat different. In other words, something had happened during that period which changed his attitude towards you. When he arrived, he told you that there had been some more air-strikes; right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I've read that in my statement, so that must be correct. It is consistent with what I remember. One -- one remark: As I told you this morning -- or I told the Prosecution this morning, I think it was the intelligence chief of -- of the unit, of the security chief, he was very unfriendly. He told us that -- that's from further incidents. It might have been the air-strikes. I don't exactly recall at this time. And he told us very clearly that we were to stay inside. We were under house arrest. We were to be guarded, and if we were to go outside we would be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you were at Grbavica, and you changed your clothes. There is a fact on the one hand, and there is your understanding of the fact on the other. Do you accept the possibility that during your transport to Pale, you might have been faced with the hostility or attacks on the part of civilians or renegades or any other individuals who might have been angry as a result of those air-strikes, and that the fact that you had to change your clothes was just a measure to protect you from any such hostilities coming from the -- from such individuals?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I can only state that any comment about that would be, well, speculation of my side. As I told you before, the -- the reactions of -- of the few Bosnian Serb people I met had been correct. In fact, our landlord was quite upset when we were taken. About the -- being forced to -- to take off our military clothes, that was clearly for me, although I don't understand Serbo-Croatian, on orders. There were a lot of phone calls about that. And in my opinion, it is totally inconsistent with Geneva law or any other law about conduct in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would have been even more against the Geneva Conventions if somebody had noticed your white clothes during your journey and if they had opened -- opened fire at you. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I was not wearing white clothes. I was wearing Dutch military uniform with the UN distinctive markings on it. And as I told you before, I don't have any reason to -- to expect -- suspect that. So it would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that moment, you were told, and you mentioned the president or the command earlier on, and during our interview you told us that the local commander at Mount Jahorina, or even before that, told you that you were a prisoner of war, and that resulted from the fact that the previous night the president of the republic had stated on TV that UNPROFOR members were prisoners of war taken by the Serb army; right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: The facts -- well, the statement that we were prisoners of war was mentioned several times during the period I was taken hostage. To me, in fact, I had quite some discussions with the guard at the radar station because, in my opinion, we were hostages because we were not being accorded the treatment due to prisoners of war in Geneva Conventions, like being used as a human shield, having to take off our uniforms, being denied protective measures, et cetera, being denied access to the Red Cross. There was quite a discussion about that, but in my opinion, the guards were told -- and I said they told me and us we were to be prisoners of war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During our conversation, we agreed that nobody had told you that you would be released if the air-strikes stopped; right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct. It was never specifically mentioned. Several times we mentioned that there were negotiations ongoing, and as I said before, several people, they stated that they hoped the situation would be resolved quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that after 16 hours you were suspected of having co-operated with NATO? Allegedly, UNPROFOR staff played the role of forward air controllers which selected targets and aimed at those targets with lasers. I'm not asking you whether you actually did that. I'm asking you whether those who had captured you suspected you of such doings?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: With the 16 hours I presume you mean on the 26th, after 16 hours when we were taken hostage. I don't know the exact time and date, but I do recall that several times it has been -- we were accused or accusations were being brought up that UNMOs had, in fact, operated as forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your affiliation to the air force of the Dutch military support their suspicions?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Not especially by me, because in my group of UNMOs, there was, for instance, also a Polish fighter pilot, or former fighter pilot. I can only state that I had never been involved nor had any training in forward air controlling and I never had any equipment. I never saw of my colleagues being involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not accusing you. I'm just asking you whether such suspicions were every brought up, whether those who had captured you ever accused you of such things?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: As I stated before, yes, the accusation has come up several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to thank you once again for having met up with the Defence and for having come to testify here, and this brings my cross-examination to an end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, at page 21 of the transcript today, Mr. Karadzic told you that there was a major Muslim offensive launched on the 1st of May and it intensified on the 15th of May, and you said, yes, there was intense shelling.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just describe what you witnessed as far as outgoing and incoming shells or other fire was concerned in relation to that period?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes. In general there were almost daily, once or twice there was shelling from the Serb side. There was a hilltop quite close to our radar station -- to our observation post, towards the city, and very rarely have I witnessed impacts into our area of responsibility of -- of any form of shelling other than small-arms fire. There was one period, I don't know -- recall the exact dates, when there was very intense shelling, but most of that time we did report incoming and outgoing shelling which was more incoming than more outgoing, of course, but we were in shelters at that time because situation was quite dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you say that very rarely have you witness the impacts into our area of responsibility, any form of shelling other than small-arms fire, which side would that have been from?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: I do remember three mortar grenades -- well, in fact, I saw them. I heard them and saw them exploding in the area of one of the nearby Serb barracks. That's three shells I recall very clearly, because that was at the start of one of the major shelling -- well, exchanges in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS HELGERS
utterances.text: Most -- most shelling, I mean, obviously in this case, was going outside from our area towards Sarajevo, the Bosniak-held area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Helgers. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal I thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my pleasure, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Edgerton will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I seek your leave to -- to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are bringing in the next witness, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if we could stay in private session for one other matter. We're wondering about whether we're likely to see Mr. Zecevic testifying next week because it's a big witness and that requires a lot of preparation, and I know you've issued a subpoena, but I was wondering if there was any likelihood that he would testify next week or whether his testimony will take place at some other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take the -- whether or not he should testify via videolink hasn't been decided yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, and we would really like to be heard on that with that witness because we feel very strongly about that. But apart from that, since there's so much uncertainty, we would wonder if the Prosecutor or the Chamber has any information as to whether it's likely that this witness will actually be testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Tieger, in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any departure from the anticipated -- that is, any deviation from the intentions of the subpoena and the selected dates, but I can -- as always, I'm happy to check quickly and see if there's more current information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would recommend you to do that. In particular, given that the setting up the videolink would require a substantial amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I've just been informed there is no change that we're aware of, and we're moving forward accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you not minded to provide with the -- provide the Chamber with the medical documents? I'll check into that. I'm not clear about it. I'll come back to it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are now in open session. Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll wait for an opportunity and respond to the Court in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we do that. Let's go back to private session briefly again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify there was no intention to signal any departure from the intention to submit medical documentation if possible, and we have been in contact with the witness. I believe he had informally received the -- the subpoena and that the anticipated provision or at least the potential provision of such documentation was anticipated after that receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we go into public session again, I would like to -- we really strongly oppose to the videolink for this particular witness and would much prefer that he -- his testimony be postponed until the time that he's able to come to The Hague and give his testimony given the importance of his testimony, but I won't argue that point now, but I would like to have the opportunity after the medical information is submitted. It seems like it's being treated almost like something that's automatic and we really don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it will not be decided automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're in open session and on the topic of videolink, I note that we received yesterday a motion for videolink for Witness KDZ041, and I would like indicate to the Chamber that we don't oppose that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We appreciate your co-operation, and that motion is granted. Good morning, Mr. Riley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Riley, first of all, could you give us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Jonathon Peter Riley.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General Riley, do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal back in April 1996 in relation to your observations and experiences as commander of the -- of a BritBat unit for UNPROFOR in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do, and that took place in the barracks at Chepstow in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you review that statement prior to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today which gave rise to the answers set out in that statement, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, could I ask that the statement of General Riley, which is 65 ter 22685, from 15 April 1996, be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2148.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll now read a summary, then, of the written evidence in P2148. General Jonathon Riley commanded the 1st Battalion of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers during their -- pardon me, during their deployment to Gorazde from February to August 1995 as part of UNPROFOR's peacekeeping mission. Their mission was to monitor and preserve the integrity of the Gorazde total exclusion zone as well as to monitor and report on the implementation of the 31 December 1994 cessation of hostilities agreement by both sides. Additionally, the BritBat unit in Gorazde was to support the safe delivery of humanitarian aid into the area. The battalion deployed three companies, two of which were located along the east and west banks of the Drina River in interpositioned observation posts and check-points along the confrontation line. Following NATO air-strikes on 25 and 26 May, relations with the Bosnian Serb forces in the immediate area deteriorated to the point where contact almost ceased. The single exception was that the witness received a radio message from the local commander, Radomir Furtula, saying that he had been ordered by General Mladic that if NATO attacked the Serbs again, he was to shell the BritBat camp as Britain was a NATO country. During the morning of 28 May 1995, the witness was contacted via Motorola by Furtula's interpreter asking him to attend what was described as an important meeting at check-point 6 at 2.00 p.m. Aware that the hostage-taking had started in Sarajevo, the witness declined. At around 2.00 p.m., he was informed that three of his observation posts on the west bank of the Drina had been invaded by large numbers of heavily armed Bosnian Serb soldiers and their crews were captured. Soon after, observation posts on the east bank of the Drina were attacked. Two withdrew under fire. The crew of a further third was captured. In total, 33 British United Nations peacekeepers were taken hostage. I'll just now, if I may, proceed with a few questions for General Riley.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps, General, we could begin by having you give us an update on your military service since your tour in Bosnia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Certainly. In 1996, I was promoted to Colonel and appointed as the Chief of Staff of the 1st Armoured Division. I returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina with NATO in 1998 as the deputy commander of division, and I remained there, in Banja Luka, until October of 1999. The following year I was appointed as the force commander -- the British force commander in Sierra Leone, where I remained until 2001. For a period then I was the director of studies at the Joint Services Staff College. In 2003, I went to Iraq where I held two appointments for two years. The second appointment, I was the divisional commander in southern Iraq. I then moved as the senior British officer in United States central command for two years. In late 2007, I went to Afghanistan as the deputy commanding general of all NATO troops, and I remained there until the beginning of 2009. Since June 2009, I've held my current appointor as director general and master of the Royal Armouries.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to go back to the statement that you gave in 1996, I'd just like to ask you a couple of brief questions. During your tour in Gorazde, did you become familiar with the Bosnian Serb military units immediately surrounding the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I did. There were elements of three army corps of the Bosnian Serb Army. There was a single brigade of the Drina Corps based in the Serb municipality of Gorazde. To the north of the enclave there were three brigades of the Romanija Sarajevo Corps with whom we had little contact except for one of those brigades whose territory was -- was passed through by our line of supply. And on other bank of the Drina River there were three brigades of Hercegovina Corps with whom we had only contact with one brigade, the Rudo Brigade. These were all light mountain brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say on the other bank of the Drina River, which bank are you referring to, the east or the west bank?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about on the -- the -- I'm so sorry. The Romanija Sarajevo Corps and the Drina Corps were located on the bank of the Drina on -- which was on the same side as the mountain of Sjenokos, which I think is the west bank, and the Hercegovina Corps on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just two small questions drawn from your written evidence. On page 3, in the last paragraph on page 3, you indicated you had been informed in advance of the air-strikes that occurred in late May 1995. Do you by any chance recall, and I recognise this is far away in time, but do you recall how far in advance that might have been?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It was no more than 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a further question on page 5, the very last paragraph on page 5 you state: "I learned that Mladic had come to visit early on," and then continued to describe some information related to that visit. And I wonder if you could date that approximately in time for us.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe that it was on or about the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to a number of documents relating to the period that your written evidence dwells upon, but before doing that, I'd just like to remind you that in your written evidence you noted that immediately following the air-strikes at Pale on 25 and 26 May 1995, relations with the Serb side deteriorated to the point where contact almost ceased. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then perhaps we could see 65 ter 20055, which is a document from General Zivanovic of the Drina Corps command, dated 25 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a translation of that document in English on the screen in front you, General?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document, which is an order to the commands of all Drina Corps units, reads, among other things, at paragraph 3 as follows: "Prevent all movement of UNPROFOR vehicles and of all other international organisations, whether individual or in convoy, and in case of their appearance in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, immediately block them and inform the corps command which will issue further orders." Now, looking at the -- first of all, do you find this order coincident in time with the reference I've just made to your written -- to your written statement, to your written evidence, where you say that the Serb side deteriorated -- relations with the Serb side deteriorated to the point where contact almost ceased?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Indeed, and it's the same day. So the order was implemented clearly immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From what you've said, then, I take it you find that this order is consistent with the situation at the time as you experienced it.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It is exactly the experience that I -- that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2149.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, relating to the hostage-taking of members of your battalion, I'd like to know, as battalion commander, did you, following their release, receive any information on their experiences?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I did. They were all interviewed following their release, and their experiences were captured. They were all asked to fill in questionnaires about their own particular experience, and I received copies of those questionnaires and a summary of findings. And much later on, I was able to meet them all, collectively and individually, at Bugojno in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you met them did you then discuss what they had experienced during their capture?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I did. I discussed matters with the one officer, the sergeant, and the junior NCOs and more senior soldiers to get an idea of how they'd been treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you just mentioned that they had all been asked to fill in questionnaires, and you received copies of those questionnaires.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask in that regard for 65 ter 19311, page 2, please. Now go over to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to questionnaires, are these the sort of questionnaires that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes. This, of course, is before the days of the internet, and these reached me by fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a questionnaire filled in by a Corporal Storey. Was he one of the BritBat members who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: He was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of information was contained in these questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It was a full summary as they recalled it of events from the moment of confrontation until the moment of release. So it would have contained what they saw of the events around their capture, what subsequently happened to them, how they were treated, and where they were taken, what they were told, and then the circumstances surrounding their release.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where did you learn that they had been taken?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean by that where they were taken and physically placed themselves, or where was I when I learned?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. You indicated in your evidence that some of the -- among the information contained in these questionnaires was information as to where they had been taken.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Indeed. They were all asked, as far as possible, to identify the locations to which they had been taken, and this information was summarised on a report by the debriefing team, and I recall seeing a map which gave -- which gave an outline of where they had all been dropped off. In addition, when I talked the matter over with the officer who had been taken, he had, as far as possible, taken measures to pair up young soldiers with more experienced soldiers or non-commissioned officers and had then tried to remember where each of them was dropped.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on now, given that answer, to 65 ter 19301, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm not seeking to tender the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned a report by a debriefing team, and the document you have on the screen in front of you is entitled "Final Debriefing Report - Gorazde Hostages," dated 3 July 1995. That is a UK document. Is this the type of debriefing report you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one, and this summarises the information that the debriefing team had assembled having interviewed all the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move over to the next page of this document, please, to give the witness a chance to review it more fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraphs 7, 8, 9, 10, and down to 16 of this document, General, we see drop points for the witnesses from Rogatica, to Sokolac, Knezina, Vlasenica, Milici, and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go back over to page 1 of the document for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 of this document notes: "The hostages were taken from the northern -- taken from the northern OPs were dropped off and detained at various locations in small groups of varying numbers on a northerly route which extended from Visegrad to Zvornik, while the hostages taken from OP2 were all taken to the same location in Bileca." Now, that's a lot of locations, General, but I wonder if, based on your tour in Bosnia, you have some familiarity with those locations and are able to identify the expanse of territory they represent?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Indeed. This represents almost the entire Drina valley on Bosnian territory, from Bileca, which, if my memory is correct, is in Herzegovina, all the way up to Zvornik, which is on the frontier between Bosnia and Serbia. So it's a stretch of between 80 and a hundred miles.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document, please, Your Honours, as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no opposition from the Defence? Yes, as a contemporaneous report we can admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go on now, very briefly, to something that's already been exhibited. P2137, which is an order from the VRS Main Staff to General Milovanovic, numbered 03/4-1037, dated 27 May 1995, on the reception and deployment of UNPROFOR members in the corps' area of responsibility. Now, General, have you seen this document in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could I ask that we move over to point 5 on this document, which is in the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, point 5 of this document directs, among other things, the command of the Drina Corps to place captured UNPROFOR troops and members of the other humanitarian organisations at the installations in its area of responsibility. Just a quick question in this regard. Is this also consistent with the experiences as you understood them of your peacekeepers who had been taken hostage?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and when I compare this document with the debriefing report and the experiences of those who were captured, it's a clear indication that this -- that this activity was being ordered and co-ordinated at a high level, because we're looking at a distribution of hostages across at least -- at least three, if not four, army corps throughout that area. And since corps commanders do not normally give orders to each other, that order has clearly come from the next level up, which is the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go, please, over to 65 ter 03903, which is an order dated 27 May 1995, from the Drina Corps command to all units, specifically referring to the order we've just looked at, P2137.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, have you had a chance to see this document in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, point 1 of this document orders the command of the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade to capture and disarm UN members who were blocked in the Sjenokos sector, confiscate their vehicles and use them as their combat hardware, and store personal weapons until further notice. That's point 1 and 2, actually. Does this order correspond with what happened to your OPs on Sjenokos as you noted in your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Indeed. And to enlarge a little on this, it corresponds with the accounts that we were able to pick up by radio from the OPs that were being surrounded at the time, and with what emerged in their debriefing, which we've already covered. I later saw some of the vehicles, I saw one personally which had been painted in Bosnian Serb camouflage and modified, and I saw another on film being used at Srebrenica. We later, about a year later, in fact, recovered the captured vehicles and the belongings of the soldiers, their helmets, their body armour, their weapons, and they were returned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if it is convenient, is it okay to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I lost track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. We'll break and we'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just if I could introduce to you Sarah Jane Dobson, from the University of Queensland in Australia, who is assisting us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome on board. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wonder if we could have that document that we left dealing with, the 65 ter number 03903, back up on the screen, please. Great. No. Not so great. Could we see an English version eventually. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, just to finish with this document, I'd like you, please, to have a look at point 3 of this Drina Corps command order which directs the command of the 5th Military Police Battalion to take over the captured UNPROFOR members and relocate them, and just by way of summary, relocate them individually, in groups of two, and in one case a group of four, to depots, corps and firing positions of corps and brigade artillery groups and command posts. Now, once again, does this order correspond with the experiences of your peacekeepers who had been taken hostage as you understood them and had reported to you?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They, as far as possible, recorded their experiences in the debriefing reports and reported that they had been placed in military installations where they were in no doubt that they were being used as human shields, which as members of a UN force with a mandate which had been put in place by the United Nations, I believe to have been highly improper, and indeed, were they prisoners of war, it would have been against the terms of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have this document, 03903, as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd just like to pull up one final document, please, 65 ter number 16505, which is a situation report from the VRS Main Staff, dated 28 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is this, General, another document that you've looked at in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then move, please, over to, I think, page 6 of the English translation of this document, and as I recall, page 3 of the original version of this document. And I may have spoken in error as regards the original version. If you could keep going. We'll look for Roman numeral II, and I think it might be page 4 in the original version. And I'm incorrect in that regard. If we could go back a bit, please. Sorry, that was my mistake, because I was looking for a Roman numeral, but in fact, on the original version it's the second paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But focusing for our purposes right now on the English translation, the last sentence in this paragraph that's headed "Situation on the Ground" reads: "During the day, the Drina Corps captured 27 members of UN forces (Englishmen) and 4 armoured vehicles." Now, could I just ask you, your statement notes -- or in your written evidence you refer to the capture of 33 members of UN forces. Do you see a discrepancy in this document, and if so, could you explain it?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, I see two discrepancies. The first is that they are described as Englishmen whereas, in fact, they were Welsh, and doubtless they were very offended at being so described. That is understandable. The other discrepancy, which is really what you refer to, is the difference between the 33 who were captured and the 27 noted here. I believe the difference relates to six soldiers who were injured when vehicles rolled off mountain roads, and these six soldiers were taken to hospital, and that accounts for the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if this might be the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was told that it is already in evidence. Could you give the -- could the Court Deputy give the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's P2138.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. Things are just moving so fast I wasn't able to keep up. Perhaps we could move to actually one further and final document, 65 ter 13392, that I don't believe has been put before the Court as yet. Could we have an English version, please. 65 ter 13392 is an order from the VRS Main Staff, dated 2 June 1995, on the release of members of UNPROFOR. Are you having difficulty locating the translation? Can you try under 65 ter 13569. I think we're -- oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, is this another document you've looked at in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you having spoken about the six soldiers who were injured when their vehicle rolled off mountain roads, I'd like to take you to paragraph 2 of this document, which is on the next page in English. This document, at paragraph 2, orders the Drina Corps command to release six detained UNPROFOR members who were being treated at the hospital of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I wonder if you see any relationship between this document and the six injured soldiers you were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do. I was made aware that the soldiers had been injured through radio conversations with a Serb army liaison officer who was located with the brigade headquarters in the Serb municipality of Gorazde, and he told me that the soldiers had been injured and had been taken to hospital and would be cared for. And I asked that since they were injured, that they should be released as soon as possible, and I later learned that they had been released, and I believe these to be the same men.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I tender this, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of General Riley in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having met with the Defence. Our meeting will certainly help us to be more efficient and to shed more light on many things. First of all, I would like to tell you that I'm very pleased with your book the "White Dragon," in which you described the tour of the Welsh Royal Fusiliers in Gorazde. I'm sorry I did not read it before our interview. With your permission, I'm going to be using it during the cross-examination. I have to say that you are an excellent writer and that in very few words you have said so much, and once again I would like to thank you for this excellent book. General, I would like to show you the last document again. It's 13569.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call it up in e-court for the benefit of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I have recalled the document just to clarify certain terminology. Here you say UNPROFOR members who were taken prisoner. In our language, when you say "prisoner," that means that the person was arrested, and when you say "detainee," that's a prisoner of war, although this "war" bit is implied rather than actually uttered. Do you agree with me? In your mind is there a distinction between a prisoner and a prisoner of war or a detainee?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
