utterances.text: A prisoner of war, as I would understand it, would be somebody who was taken captive from an opposing force, and since we were members of an international force not opposed to either side, I do not believe that members of my battalion could have been taken prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need to clarify the terminology, and the interpreters can confirm for the Trial Chamber that a prisoner is somebody who was arrested for a crime committed in civilian life, whereas a prisoner of war is a result of war. And now, Witness, I would like to see not if General Zivanovic is right or not, but let's see how the Drina Corps perceives you, not you personally but NATO and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P2149 to illustrate that. The document has just been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the part which starts with the words "NATO aircraft," where it says that on the 25th of May, 1995, in the afternoon, NATO aircraft, which are a part of UNPROFOR, conducted operations against facilities of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then a description follows, and now it says the Army of Republika Srpska responded by conducting operations against selected targets. However, Muslim forces in co-operation with UNPROFOR are expected to continue operations against military targets in Republika Srpska in order to raise the level of combat readiness in units to the highest level and to successfully repel attacks and so on and so forth. Do you see that the commander of the Drina Corps actually sees a complete unity or a complete alliance between UNPROFOR, NATO, and Muslim rebels?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The commander of that corps may choose to present matters in that way, but that is not, in fact, a reflection of the true situation. NATO aircraft were not part of UNPROFOR. They were acting in support of UNPROFOR. And to my knowledge, there was never any occasion, certainly in the area that I was deployed, where our forces would have fought alongside either the Bosnian Muslim government forces or any other force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not questioning the accuracy of this. This is just the perception of the Serbian Army. Do you know that on the 27th, UNPROFOR sent a report, maybe it was on the 28th, and in that report it stated that the Muslim army started exploiting the results of NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a reference for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give the reference, Mr. Karadzic, for that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a report or a telegram sent on the 28th of May. I believe that the telegram has already been admitted. We had it displayed earlier on, and in that telegram it says that the Muslim forces -- maybe by the end we will be able to locate the document, but in any case, it has already been shown in this courtroom. UNPROFOR reported from the ground and said that the Muslim forces had started exploiting the results of NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, when asked by the Prosecution, you are expected to give the reference to that document instead of making a lengthy statement on your own. I take it you do not have the reference with you at this moment. Then I think you can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact, did you know, General, that the Muslim side had celebrated NATO air-strikes on Serb positions and hailed them, as a matter of fact, and that they launched activities in order to make the most of the results of those air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Since no NATO air-strikes had taken place in or around Gorazde within my area of responsibility, I'm not aware of any such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to your statement? You were familiar with the situation in Gorazde as it was in 1994, and you speak about that in the fourth paragraph of your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Is it possible to see the statement on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can print out the statement of the witness, why don't we give them in hard copy, but in the meantime, we can upload his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the statement. We need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "In the spring of 1994." You said that there had been fierce battles around the city between Muslim and Serb forces, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we collapse the Serbian version and zoom in to the English version. Yes. I think it will be more convenient for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, you have no problem because you have it with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were informed -- or, rather, you knew where you were headed for, and you knew that there had been fierce battles around the city after the first round of air-strikes; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I had been briefed during our preparation for the tour, and conversations with people on both sides around the area informed me that that had been the case. I could see physical evidence of fighting, but clearly, I was not there on the ground and cannot verify any details personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 in the same statement, I hope you have it in hard copy, you say that in 1995, in the month of May, when you were already there, you had received information from various sources, and you will find it in the fourth paragraph of your statement. [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] May was a busy month." [Interpretation] Which showed that the legal of troops in that area on both sides was more or less equal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday during our conversation, we arrived at the conclusion -- or, rather, it was your conclusion that there were about 5 to 6.000 troops in the 81st Division in Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: No. We believe that there was somewhere between 8 and 11.000 soldiers in the 81st Division, of whom the divisional commander had weapons for about 6.500. That was our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you take into account the fact that they operated in shifts, it would be fair to conclude that each soldier was equipped with arms when they were actually on duty.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the 81st Division divided into brigades, companies, and lower-ranked units?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: As far as we could understand, the division was divided into five light brigades which were assigned to ground-holding in various sectors, and they had one manoeuvre brigade called the Manevarska Brigade. Within each brigade there would usually be at least three battalions which would be divided into three or four companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They also had their separate staffs as well as logistics bases, staff units, and so on and so forth; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the size of the enclave, do you believe that that was a rather dense level of militarisation in that enclave?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe that it -- the defenders had mobilised all the resources that they could, as any prudent military commander would in order to assure the defence of their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I had in mind the size of the area and the number of 11.000 troops. I would say that they were quite densely deployed, that the area was quite heavily militarised; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: As you yourself just said, they operated in shifts, so that the maximum that might be on duty at any one time would be considerably less than that, 6.500. And given the size of the enclave, no, I do not believe that that is an overly dense deployment. When I made an assessment of what we needed should the UN or even NATO have to defend this area rather than deter, I came to the view that it would require at least one division with supporting troops from corps level, which would be, if anything, more than the Bosnian side had deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's not speculate. I'm not a soldier. Am I right in saying defenders need few troops than are needed by those who attack the area, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If one side were to defend itself and the other side to attack the area, would you say that those who attacked the area would need more troops than the defenders?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand now. It is usually considered that if the troops are equipped to an equal level, a defender -- I'm sorry, an attacker would be wise to muster at least 3:1 in terms of superiority. However, the attacker has the ability to concentrate force against one particular point if he has a force ratio which is in overall terms inferior. He is able to achieve a local superiority. And of course, in the case of Gorazde, the 81st Division had very little in the way of heavy weapons, such as mortars, artillery and tanks, and I believe that the Serb side held an extreme superiority in those heavy weapons which would serve to build up the required superiority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But even what they had in terms of heavy weapons and mortars, they certainly didn't keep that on the front line [indiscernible] kept it behind the lines in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Many of the heavy weapons that I observed on the Bosnian side were mortars, which have a limited range of only up to 5 kilometres. I only saw one or two field artillery pieces and I only ever saw one tank. So some of them would have been behind the front line. The smaller mortars would have been very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 you say -- or, rather, during our interview you agreed, and you also mentioned it in the book, that Serbs were around 12.500 in Gorazde and that they had been driven out of their own neighbourhoods as well as the suburbs on the right bank of the Drina River; correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I was told that by people from both communities, and since the account was much the same from both communities, I believed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also observed that they only escaped across the confrontation line, and outside the confrontation line there were Serb villages who received these refugees, and these refugees continued to fight around Gorazde. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case. And inside the enclave, there were also large numbers of refugees from the other community who in the same way resisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3, we're again on page 3, last paragraph, says that you had been warned in advance about NATO air-strikes which occurred in the end of May, and you made sure that in the period before the air-strikes your liaison officer did not cross the confrontation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Correct. As I answered earlier, the warning about air-strikes was no more than 24 hours ahead of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, you say that the situation -- that's paragraph 4. You say that on the 29th of May, 30th, 31st, and 1st of June, the situation deteriorated because of heavy fighting all around you; correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down on page 6, you say that the Serb side attacked the Hercegovina Corps on the right bank, trying to take that area on the right-hand side and east of the Drina River, and that you helped them. [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] I think it is no exaggeration to say that our defence of the east bank until the Muslims could mobilise and secure Mala Biserna," the hill, right, on the right bank?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It is an important hill, the position of which dominates the town, the safe area and total exclusion zone. I considered it vital ground to be held, and if it was not held by me or by the defenders, then the safe area was no longer safe and that I would be failing in my mission if that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "[In English] It is not an exaggeration that this action has saved the town. Had we been pushed off, the Serbs could have destroyed Gorazde with fire."

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's still some kind of speculation. Do you know that it was very difficult to stop Serbs 50 metres from their own homes, from freeing them? Do you know that these situations were very emotionally charged?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: As the commander responsible for deterring attacks on the safe area and for maintaining the total exclusion zone, I'm afraid I had not the luxury of emotion. I was given a mission which I was obliged to fulfil to the best of my ability. And on that day, it was clear to me that my soldiers were being attacked very heavily by the Hercegovina Corps side, and having formed the professional view that the Mala Biserna feature was vital to the security of the safe area, I could do nothing else but to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you believe that it was your mandate to repel Serb attacks against Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: What my mission said was to deter attacks on the safe area. My rules of engagement allowed me to use lethal force if I was attacked to defend myself and our mission, which is what, in fact, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, there is a misunderstanding there between the UNPROFOR and the Serb side in Bosnia. To defend oneself and one's mission are two different things. Do you remember that General Mladic always used to say, "If my soldiers shoot at you, feel free to return fire"? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, we seemed to agree yesterday that you were neither able to nor did you prevent the Muslim division from attacking Serbian villages around Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we did agree that. During the period of time up until this episode began in May, I was not aware that there had been any Bosnian government forces, Muslim forces, attacks from out of the enclave. Had I known of any, I would have done my best to prevent them. The attacks that took place in this area were counter-attacks, and they all took place after the total exclusion zone had been violated by the attacks of the Serb side on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will have to present a number, a great number of documents where the Serb side claims and proves that those were, in fact, Serb counter-attacks in response to attacks from the enclave. But you couldn't, nor did you ever prevent such attacks from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was an unnecessary statement on your part. Please refrain from making such statements. I will indicate whenever you make them. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the fact remains that in all that time you were there, you never prevented any action by the 81st Division against Serb settlements.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is a fact, and therefore it does not remain, as I've said before. Until the 28th of May, I know of no attack that took place by the 81st Division out of the enclave, and therefore there was nothing for me to prevent. Had I become aware of any event, and I believe I would, then I would have done my best to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say on page 6 that during your tenure there, that the Royal Wales Battalion escorted about 78 convoys into Gorazde and it fought 60 separate combat incidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case, then, in the light of the fact that NATO was making air-strikes at the invitation of the UNPROFOR commander, that we can view this paragraph written by Zivanovic where he says that his corps was attacked by the joint forces of NATO and the Muslim forces? Perhaps not in so many words. Perhaps it was phrased differently.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That was certainly not the case in my area of responsibility, which is the only area on which I'm able to comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may, that question is -- actually, I wasn't quite quick enough. It's assuming facts not in evidence, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now the issue's moot in light of the witness's answer. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to shed some light on the structure of the UNPROFOR forces in Gorazde, namely the British Battalion. Were there any SAS members in that BritBat?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were a total of eight divided into two teams of four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6 we saw there were about 60 separate combat incidents. Did you also have any combat incidents against the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You mean the Bosnian government Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes. On at least two occasions. On one occasion, a convoy of vehicles was fired on by the Bosnian side in the area of Osojnica bridge. This was in late April. And towards the very end of my mission, when the British government had announced that at the termination of our tour of duty we would not be replaced, and during the initial period of withdrawal, we were attacked in some force by elements of the Bosnian government army. I do not believe this to have been an official policy, I believe it to have been a local initiative, but the attack did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph, the fifth paragraph on page 6, you say that on August 28, news came that NATO had begun air-strikes -- no. In fact, they withdrew on the 28th of August, but you received news, and you say: "[In English] This had the potential to attract Serb reprisal in response. Had this occurred, we would have been stranded in Gorazde. Additionally, we had been warned we were facing a serious attack by BH renegades who were redoubling their efforts to foil our retreat. We had been guaranteed the assistance of General Mladic in a meeting he had with General Smith and myself. Mladic was true to his word. Despite fierce Muslim attack aim at blocking our movement, we were able to extract from Gorazde and out through Serbian territory without a loss of a single life." [Interpretation] Is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, there are two issues there, I think. The first is that we were aware, as we began the final phase of our withdrawal, that we faced the likelihood of another Bosnian side renegade attack. In the first attack we had killed some of their soldiers, and we knew that their families, in particular, wanted revenge, and for that reason I did not wish to get embroiled in a large battle and wished to disengage and leave the area in accordance with my orders. We also knew that there had been an incident in Sarajevo, but I did not know the details, and I did not know that the -- that there were NATO air-strikes at that point, because those air-strikes did not take place until after we had arrived in Belgrade, in Beograd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With your leave, we will go through your book to identify these various incidents. Did the Royal Welsh Fusiliers co-ordinate with the Muslim army to secure UNPROFOR members on the right bank so that Serbs do not capture them? Did you have that kind of co-operation with them?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: No, we did not co-operate with them. We held liaison with them, as indeed we had liaison with the Serb side. But as a UN force, we were there to -- in support of the UN mandated mission and not to fight alongside or co-ordinate with either of the factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But still, you secured the right bank for them, preventing Serbs from freeing their own homes. Were they grateful to you for keeping the right bank safe for them when they were unable to resist?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The defence of the right bank was nothing to do with preventing Serbs from freeing their homes, as you put it. It was everything to do with deterring attacks on the safe area, with responding to a violent attack mounted on my force there, and preserving the total exclusion zone. I did not have the force available and the weaponry available to hold that ground, which I've already described as vital, for an extended period, and I knew that the only people who could defend it was the Bosnian Army, and therefore I had a responsibility to defend it as long as I could and then let that force from the Bosnian Army assume the defence. It is, after all, the responsibility -- the first responsibility of any government to defend its own people, and you know that, and that's what I had to do. It was all to do with the safe area and the security of the civilian population in that safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you know almost all the Serbs out of those 12.500 who stayed in Gorazde -- you probably know how many stayed behind, and you probably knew them all.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I was aware of 11 ethnic Serb people in the enclave, and I didn't know them. There may have been more, but I was only aware of 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of these eight SAS members, were there any forward air controllers?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Both of the two teams of four contained two men who were trained as forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now call up 1D3036. That's your book that I can only praise, and I feel there are not enough compliments. Is this the cover page?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page numbering is different in e-court, so I kindly ask for everyone's indulgence while I find the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you by any chance have a hard copy of the book?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let's proceed with the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 8 of the book, and it could be 4 or 5 in e-court. Pages 8 and 9. Can we turn to those pages. That's the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, you say that the -- that a 500-strong UN garrison lay some 80 miles from the nearest UN troops, and that UN garrison was maintained there with the consent of both Bosnian and Serbs, something not always understood at home. In Britain, the nature of these relations were not sufficiently understood in Britain. And because of the need to maintain consent for its presence, its convoys are liable for inspection by the Serbs on their route.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say that many convoys have indeed passed. Do you agree that your presence there had the consent of both sides?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I suppose you agree that under international law, we were entitled to set conditions under which aid would pass to the other side through our territory.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: If that was agreed with the UN, that is so. Consent from both sides, however, is rarely an absolute, in my experience. It is a relative. It varies from time to time, depending on the circumstances, and it varies at different levels of a command. At your level, I'm in no doubt that you had reached agreement and consented to the force. That did not mean that all of your subordinates necessarily agreed with that and would do anything other than make it difficult for these supply convoys to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see page 11. And I believe you will agree that soldiers frequently object to the decisions of politicians in -- in military matters. Isn't that the case in all armies?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: They may not like it, but in every army that I've served in, orders are orders, and the political element has primacy, and soldiers do as they're instructed by their political masters or they cease to be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the right-hand side, page 11, the second paragraph which starts with "On April 16th." And now in this paragraph you were saying that Srebrenica was declared a UN safe area. "[In English] ... was not matched by resources for their defence, nor was the disarmament plan ever poorly implemented -- properly implemented." [Interpretation] Do you remember that when it comes to Gorazde, no agreement was ever reached on the boundaries of the safe area, nor was the area every properly demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: To deal with the disarmament and demilitarisation aspect first, as I understand it, the area was not determined or described as a safe haven, because the conditions for being a safe haven are a guarantee of complete security in return for total demilitarisation. The area was designated as a safe area. There was indeed no geographical description of that. I was never able to get any description, and nor was General Smith. His guidance to me was what I went on and his guidance to me was that the purpose of the safe area was to protect the civilian population so far as it is possible to do so in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the following two pages, 12 and 13. I would like to draw your attention to page 13, the last paragraph thereof. "[In English] Then came the real business. If any further Muslim fire took place, this would be the signal for the Serbs to fire on the town." [Interpretation] You knew that fire was opened from within the town and that Serbs returned fire.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I think as my account there makes plain, we were quite sure that fire had not been opened from the town, that none of our observation posts or liaison teams had heard any such fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the paragraph says differently; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: No, I don't think it does. I think what it reports is an exchange of views between me and the Serb side in which an accusation was made from the Serb side that fire had been opened from inside the town. I did not believe that to have been the case, and I made it clear that it had been wrong for the Bosnian side to use me, the UN force, as a shield from which to launch aggression, and I formed the view that this accusation was a false one and was going to form the basis of a justification for the shelling of the safe area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to page 16. One more, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember Podkovacev Dol as a locality. I would like to draw your attention to this: "[In English] The patrol had been out for two days. Based on an abandoned house in the village Podkovacev Dol and was actually packing its kits ready to leave when a sniper fired at the sentry. The sentry at once returned the fire in response. A number of Serb positions opened up with heavy MG fires. So heavy was the fire that the house began to disintegrate. The patrol commander ... Nightingale deployed the whole patrol to suppress the hostile fire ..." [Interpretation] And then on the following page. Whose sniper was it that provoked that response on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should remain on that page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we should remain on that page, page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, was it ever established whose sniper provoked your response to which the Serbs opened fire from heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You'd have to question Lieutenant Nightingale or one of the soldiers who was actually present since I am -- since I am summarising their account. They, however, were very clear that the fire had come from the Serb side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, General, if that had come from the Serb side, why didn't they start with the heavy artillery fire? Were the two lines close to each other in that area?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Well, since neither of us was present, I don't think that we can accurately engage in a reconstruction of this engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 17 you say this: "[In English] I can only guess that Hugh Nightingale's patrol must have killed some Serbs." [Interpretation] However, let's agree that we cannot establish that. It seems to me, however, that the Serb side was taken by surprise when you opened fire at them, that the sniper hadn't been theirs and that's why they responded so fiercely. And now, General, on page 17, where it says after about an hour reinforcements arrived, along with the company commander, Major Philip Jones. And then the crisis escalated, and you tried to exchange messages with the Serb side. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember contacting the liaison officer in the brigade headquarters in the Serb municipality of Gorazde and asking him to relay the message to the brigade commander concerned, who was in a different corps, telling him that there was an engagement in progress with the UN force and that it should cease. And the message I got back was that the brigade commander concerned knew that it was the UN force and did not care and would not stop the engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously they did kill some Serbs, and that's why the whole thing continued. General, did it ever happen that your troops found themselves among the Muslim troops on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Not -- no. When we patrolled, we patrolled between the lines. The observation posts were between the lines, and to reach the observation posts we would merely pass through either the Bosnian lines or indeed the Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I indicated, Mr. Karadzic, I have to intervene this time again. You made a statement which is unanswered by the witness. General, the witness said -- the accused said, "Obviously they did kill some Serbs, and that's why the whole thing continued." Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said in the account which is written there, what I said was I can only guess that. So it was -- I was trying to rationalise why the next patrol should have come under such heavy fire immediately, and I can only believe that the previous engagement resulted in a death on the Serb side and that, therefore, they wished to take revenge. But that is a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like us to look at pages 24 and 25. Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the passage under the asterisks. "[In English] Just on the southern side of Gorazde is a village called Vitkovici." [Interpretation] And now you continue to explain that many Muslims live there, there were both soldiers and civilians, and that one of the largest schools in the district was there. Just across the Drina were the Serb lines, which overlooked the village, and in many cases occupied by soldiers who had lived in Vitkovici but were forced to leave. And you continue to say: "[In English] It is a place where feelings run high."

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I meant when I spoke about emotions. I did not have in mind the professionals of the Welsh Fusiliers. Do you agree with me that it was difficult to manage and control people who could see their houses across the confrontation line, and you did notice that feelings run high over there?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Feelings may have run high, but international law prevents attacks on -- I'm sorry, prohibits attacks by military forces on civilians, and if any soldiers were attacking civilians, which was the case here, then the military commanders on the spot should have taken steps to prevent it by removing, perhaps, the soldiers whose feelings were running high and replacing them with others who could be more dispassionate. I do not accept that any amount of emotion justifies the action that was being taken in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agree, General, but do you also agree that soldiers, both on the Muslim and Serb sides, that they had been civilians only until yesterday and that they simply wanted to defend their houses? They were not professional troops. And you will agree that there is a big difference between professionals and former civilians?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do not believe that the law would make such a distinction. If somebody is wearing a uniform and under military discipline, they're subject to military law. And everybody, whether they're a military person or civilian, is surely subject to international law and bound to obey -- and bound to obey it, just as in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, with all due respect, I'm not trying to justify anything. I'm just trying to understand or make both of us understand what kind of troops there were on both sides. Were they professionals or former civilians who fought for their houses? Did you encounter situations where people fought in civilian clothes, not in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I sometimes saw a mixture of military and civilian clothes, but I do not recall seeing in the Gorazde area anybody in the line on either side who was wearing only civilian clothes. I should qualify that. I shouldn't say that I never saw anybody armed on either side who was in civilian clothes. I did see working parties digging trenches on both sides wearing civilian clothes, but they were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at page 38 -- or, rather, pages 38 and 39 in your book. The end of the passage which starts with: "Because of the fuel situation ..." "[In English] Because of the fuel situation, resupply of the OPs and change all the -- of personnel had to be done on foot by the -- and the Serbs have taken to engage patrols with small-arm fire. This is unlikely to be a co-ordinated policy. More likely is that usual mix of indiscipline, drink, and boredom."

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpretation. That's why I paused. My question is this: Does this reflect the truth, and does this corroborate the fact that the troops were not professional troops but, rather, civilian reservists?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It -- it probably does and I would agree with you that far, but if you are suggesting that that makes it somehow acceptable, then we must disagree, and I would have said in this case it was the responsibility of the many professional officers that I knew to be with the Serb forces to have prevented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, General, this is not to justify things but an attempt to understand the whole situation, and I see that you also noticed that those were just localised incidents and not something that had come as a co-ordinated policy from a central level.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: At this stage, which is April, yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we go to page 41. On the 14th of May, 1995, you say this: [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] ... that the Croatian attack caused strong feelings among the Serbs where Slavonia was a designated UN protected area, and the Serbs' anger was caused by the failure of the United Nations as they see it to deter or prevent the attack. The Croatian -- Croatian use of the air-strikes caused special anger, and the Serbs pointed out that if they had used aircraft, NATO would have been quick to respond. Clearly the Serbs see a parallel between impasse in Croatia and the east Bosnia enclaves and perceive the UN to be acting in a way which is not impartial. One can see the Serb point of view, and it -- it has merit. The answer are, of course, that the UN mandate is quite different in Croatia from that in east Bosnia and that the UN is not in former Yugoslavia to enforce anything." [Interpretation] Do you agree, General, as a good writer and as a good general, that there are no minor injustices as opposed to major injustices, that each injustice is actually a major one, and that the Serbs believed that they were subject to a major injustice only two weeks after the fall of Western Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: As I said in that account, I can understand the Serb point of view, and I would go with you on the point that you -- that all sides in a dispute have a right to the -- the same sort of response provided that the legal mandate is the same, and indeed that any injustice seems like a major injustice when you are upon the receiving end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we go to pages 44 and 45. The last paragraph on the left-hand side, page 44. [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] As the vehicle drove under the old railway bridge at Osanice, the Serbs opened fire from bunker position on high ground across the Drina. Many rounds struck at Saxons, so the vehicle commanders closed down their hatches and returned the fire. Moments later, the Muslims joined in and fired a rocket-propelled RPG-7 grenade at the first Saxon. This fortunately missed and it exploded on the road some 15 metres from in front of the vehicle. The commander, Lieutenant Llewellyn, and his second in command, Corporal Parry, then had the difficult task of suppressing the hostile fire, while also using their vehicle to shield the unarmoured police Land Rover from the heavy fighting -- heavy weight of incoming fire." [Interpretation] And then the next paragraph: "[In English] It is always regrettable when soldiers on peacekeeping duty have to engage either side, but when an outrageous and unprovoked attack like this is made, there can be no alternative but to respond in a robust and professional manner. The actions of the patrol were of the highest order and made possible the safe extractions of the civilian police from one of the most hazardous places in Bosnia. It is also clear that the -- this attack was co-ordinated and planned by the Serbs and probably had the sanction of at least a brigade commander. The action by the Muslims, whom we are here to assist and at whose request this action was carried out, was nothing short of disgraceful." [Interpretation] General, you were helping the civilian police here, and you saved them from the action of -- of the police; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: This -- first of all, could I point out that this is an account written by Major Richard Westley and not by me, and secondly, that the escort was being provided to the United Nations civilian police and not the Bosnian civil police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Bosnian police or the Muslim police, rather, actually was the cause of most harm for the civilians, the Serb civilians who had fled Gorazde and that the police always engaged in combat, that the police was part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you've -- you've presented me with an account by another officer of a particular episode which involves the UN civil police and not the Bosnian civil police, so I'm unclear as to why you're asking me now about the Bosnian police who were not involved in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't say here that it was the UN civil police. Were there any UN civil police in Gorazde at all?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: If you'd go, please, to the third line of the first paragraph of that -- of that account, "Attack on Osanice," you will see that it says: "On May the 17th, B Company was asked to escort a UN civilian police vehicle from Gorazde to Osanice."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, yes. Now I see it. And do you know that the Bosnian police engaged in combat and that it was actually the Muslim police that had chased Serbs out of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Since that took place before my presence on the ground, I can neither confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we go to the following page. Your soldiers were injured because the vehicle actually swerved off the road; right? "[In English] The captured soldiers were not threatened and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we on the correct page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the left-hand side, in the middle, it says: "[In English] The captured soldiers were not threatened and were allowed to collect their equipment before being taken and escorted to the Serb headquarter in Visegrad. En route, one of the Saxon vehicles slid out of the road, injuring six British and one Serb soldier." [Interpretation] Is that correct? Was that the cause of injury; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. That was my understanding at the time, and it was confirmed in the debriefing reports of the soldiers concerned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time to take a break. How much longer do you have after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how much time have I used so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't checked it yet. In any event, then we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't use all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- introduce to the Chamber Amina Noor, who is a student at the University of Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, I was told that you have spent so far an hour and 20 minutes. You will have about 40 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe I'll manage even earlier and then it's my treat to the Prosecution. I'll give them a couple of minutes from my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, would you kindly look at the next page on the screen, the page on the right, number 47, where you talk about 33 fusiliers who were taken captive [In English] not hostage. [Interpretation] That's what we say, captive, not hostage. And you say there were no victims, no one injured apart from the six who got injured in a car accident. "[In English] The next few days we were able to keep a rough track on them through the Serb liaison officer until, after five days, the first 11 were released. I spoke to them once they had reached Split, and all confirmed that they had been treated correctly, well looked after, and not threatened. Those injured in the vehicle accident received proper medical care. I have been informed this morning that a further 17 have been released, and I hope to speak to them shortly. I am quite certain the remaining five are in no danger and that they will be -- they will in due course be freed." [Interpretation] Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it follows from the book that you were fairly certain that your men were in no danger at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I have never had any issue with the way that they were treated, and I never had any reason to suppose that they would be harmed by the Serb soldiers who held them captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] I'm afraid I've lost some pages. I ask you for the indulgence, a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've found it. The book's excellent, but it's not very well bound, so I'm losing pages all the time. Can we now see page 67, please, 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you say here that you were confident that: "[In English] ... the business of our withdrawal was soon settled. The Serbs would assist us to withdraw via Belgrade. General Mladic gave the orders at once and appointed a liaison officer, asking of us only that we remove all the weapons and vehicles which had been brought in since the arrival of the Duke of Wellington's Regiment in April 1994. To this readily agreed since it was in any case our intention. We then adjourned for some Serb hospitality, a magnificent lunch and so --" no problem, "and to date, Mladic has been true to his words." [Interpretation] Now the next example. "[In English] I was less certain about the reaction of Muslim side and, indeed, no sooner had the first convoy of loaders arrived to begin the removal of heavy plants and vehicles, when obstruction began. Muslim government ministers even went so far as to suggest publicly that the British Battalion on which the enclave has depended for every mouthful of food during the past year and a half would only be allowed to leave if all the vehicles and weapons, the property of our government no less, were placed in a weapons control point." [Interpretation] Now let me not read this whole paragraph. You had problems with the Muslim side that demanded your equipment and the property of your government to be left behind; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That's what they demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Army of Republika Srpska continually asked that the UNPROFOR refrain from bringing in too many vehicles, too much ammunition and fuel into the enclave precisely because we feared that, and eventually our fears materialised? That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I recall always being under restriction for the amount of supply as I could get to keep my operations going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but doesn't this paragraph clearly show that the Serbian Army's fears that Muslims might abuse your equipment were justified?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I think that it does not justify interfering with necessary supply to a UN force, even though I would accept that they were fearful that equipment could be stolen and misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did something similar happen also to the Ukrainian Battalion? Their equipment was taken over by the Muslims and turned against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That is indeed the case. The Ukrainians allowed themselves to be surrounded and disarmed, and their vehicles and weapons were indeed taken by the Muslim side, something which I was very angry about, as the force commander, but was unable to reverse. And I was determined, absolutely determined, that that was not going to happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here that the Serb liaison officer asked you by radio if you needed any assistance, and you thought it was a joke, but do you accept that from his point of view it was serious and honest?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- what the account says was not that I thought it was a joke, because I was quite sure that he was serious, but it was black comedy, indeed, that after the hostage-taking and the fighting that had gone on earlier that I should -- I should go so far as to ask one faction to join with me in fighting another. I was not there to do that, and the last thing I wanted was to be the catalyst for more fighting. So I replied that it would be best if the Serb side remained out of this particular affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 65 -- if we can see that page. That's the page on the right. Could you please look at the last two paragraphs. "Actually, this incident is in keeping with the attitude being displayed by the Bosnian Muslims towards the UN all over the country. [In English] Convoys obstructed, even those carrying aid. Bases blocked, soldiers threatened. Here in Gorazde we have experienced all sort of harassment. Not from the Serbs but from the people who depended on us to risk our lives, breaching the Serbs' mine fields every time a UNHCR convoy comes in. This is conveniently overlooked. But this is nothing when compared to the continued harassment of the Ukrainians." [Interpretation] And then the last sentence. "[In English] It gives some idea, I think, of the almost intractable problems which have to be solved every day in the face of unbelievable ingratitude and deceit." [Interpretation] Now, is that the painful part of your experience of that departure from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: It's one of many painful memories of a painful time, and as I think the account makes clear, I was extremely angry, and indeed, I think everybody was, at the attitude of the Bosnian side in return for what we had -- what our country and the UN had done. I can only believe that they felt in some way that they were being abandoned and that this policy might help to change the situation to their advantage, but it was, in my view, a very misguided way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that all these members of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers who had been captured were at that time in active service?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand what you mean. All the soldiers who were captured during the hostage-taking episode in May or -- or are we talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean everything that you just said except the reference to "hostage." Were all your men at that point in active service?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were all regular soldiers, professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of your soldiers who had been taken prisoner -- did Karl Roberts, in fact, tell you that during his detention he had been informed by the Serbs that he was a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: He did report that he was a prisoner of war. That does not make him so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, but it's not in dispute that he had been informed by the Serbs that he had the status of prisoner of war; right?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The fact that he was told that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General. I hope we will not be seeing each other in the next war, because there will be no next war. It was a pleasure to talk to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Edgerton, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just on one small point, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, at page 68 of the transcript of today's proceedings, do you recall discussing your patrols engaging with Bosnian Serb forces in small-arms fire exchanges and Dr. Karadzic saying the following: "General, this is not to justify things but an attempt to understand the whole situation, and I see that you also noticed that those were just localised incidents and not something that had come as a co-ordinated policy from central level." And your answer was: "At this stage, which is April, I would agree with that." Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the situation you were discussing then change after April?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, during the hostage-taking that took place in May, it was clear from the sequence of events and the reports that I received afterwards and what we have seen subsequently from what happened to those people who were captured, that that aggression must have been co-ordinated at a higher level and was not simply a localised incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. One thing I wanted to clarify with you, Mr. Karadzic, is that is it your intention not to tender those parts put to the witness from the book authored by the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, and thank you for reminding me. I would rather like to tender these passages, and if the Trial Chamber doesn't mind, perhaps we could tender the whole book, but at least those pages that I read from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'd object to the whole book, Your Honour, but no objection with respect to those pages. I just wanted to note that pages 38 and 39 don't have any date reference on them, and perhaps it might be useful to all of us if we could get a couple of pages further than that that might indicate the date of that page or that entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that could be arranged outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so. Page 24 and 25, and I think page 15 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no position from the Defence on -- so that will be done. So that will be given the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D678.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that concludes your evidence, General Riley. I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go and please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, where are we in terms of witness scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have no witness available for the remainder of the day, Your Honour, and in fact, the next witness will not be ready to proceed until Friday morning. That's a consequence, as the Court I'm sure is aware, of the fact that KDZ200 fell ill and was unable to testify, and in addition to the pace, rather unprecedented, of the proceedings which could not be anticipated, and it was too late to accelerate the testimony of any additional witness. Before we adjourn, however, I would like to move into private session to continue a discussion raised earlier also in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with the scheduling issue first. You referred to two circumstances. I have -- were you not put on notice as to those such circumstances in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I would say at best the Prosecution was advised of the possibility that there could be some acceleration of the pace, but indeed, to the extent that would have been a meaningful signal, and I would say for purposes of witness rescheduling, something as tentative as the communication we received late last week could not be held to do so, that was largely contradicted by another signal we had during the course of -- of a witness interview when the scheduling anticipated for the first two witnesses by the Prosecution earlier was confirmed by the Defence. So I think it would be an error to suggest that we were put on notice that the pace of the proceedings as we've experienced it this week was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We were concerned about the fact that we lost about an hour and today -- another hour today, and we are losing about five hours tomorrow. The Chamber understands the difficulties inherent in the process of scheduling witnesses, and there are, of course, particular circumstances this week which resulted in such a loss. However, can I emphasise at this moment that it is the Prosecution's responsibility to ensure that there are sufficient witnesses here so that we do not have such unanticipated breaks, taking into account all of the information available concerning the expected time for cross-examination. So I wanted to give you notice in advance that in the future, should we find ourselves in a position where we cannot sit because of the absence of witnesses, without good cause, there may be situations in which the Chamber will ask the Registry to count some or all the time lost against the Prosecution's overall time allocation of 300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I certainly understand that as a note of general concern on the part of the Court. I can advise the Court that it doesn't, as a general principle, alert the Prosecution to anything it wasn't aware of and hasn't focused on diligently since the commencement of these proceedings. I hope it's no more than a note of general concern about time lost and not a reflection of this particular incident, because the unanticipated loss of time in this instance was the result of wholly unanticipated factors that were outside, clearly outside the Prosecution's control. So I didn't understand the Court to be suggesting otherwise. Just a reminder that everyone's concerned about time and everyone should do their utmost to ensure that we use our time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session? Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Could I add something? The interviews I had with these witnesses helped me to shorten my examination, and I believe part of the problem lies therein, part of the problem we have with the surplus of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there are other matters to be raised, the hearing is now adjourned. We will resume on Friday at 9.00. And one further notice: I think that should be -- should have been arranged, but that can be arranged. On Monday next week, I'm giving you prior notice, we will be sitting from 2.30 to 6.30. And on Tuesday, we will be sitting at the regular time, from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For me, regular is afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
